title: What Prince William Actually Does as Prince of Wales — 2026 Explained
excerpt: Prince William's role has changed more than most people realise. Duchy of Cornwall, Earthshot, homelessness work — what the job actually involves in 2026.
author: StarScoop Daily Staff
imageAlt: Prince William, Prince of Wales at a State Banquet — royal duties 2026
metaDescription: What does Prince William do as Prince of Wales? Duchy of Cornwall income, Earthshot Prize, homelessness work and his royal duties explained for 2026.
content:
Most people know Prince William is next in line to the throne. Far fewer could say what the job actually involves day to day — and it has changed considerably since he inherited the title.

Here's what being Prince of Wales genuinely means in 2026: the money, the causes, the constitutional position, and where he's chosen to differ from his father.

The Duchy of Cornwall — Where the Money Comes From

The Prince of Wales does not receive a salary. His income comes from the Duchy of Cornwall — a private estate established in 1337 to provide for the heir to the throne.

The Duchy is substantial. It holds land, property and commercial interests across England, and the annual surplus funds the Prince and Princess of Wales's official duties, their household, and their private life.

This arrangement attracts consistent scrutiny, and reasonably so. The Duchy occupies an unusual position — it is described as a private estate but exists because of a constitutional role, and it has faced questions over its tax status and its commercial dealings. William has reportedly pushed for greater transparency in how it operates than existed previously.

The practical point for readers: when you see the Wales family's official engagements, the Duchy is what pays for them, not the taxpayer directly.

The Earthshot Prize — His Signature Project

If William has one initiative that defines his public role, it's the Earthshot Prize.

Launched in 2020, it awards substantial funding each year across five categories to solutions addressing environmental problems — restoring nature, cleaning air, reviving oceans, eliminating waste, and fixing the climate. Winners receive £1 million each to scale their work.

The framing is deliberately optimistic, which is the interesting choice. Environmental campaigning has historically leaned on alarm. Earthshot is structured around solutions and prize money — closer to a venture competition than a protest movement.

That approach lets William engage with climate as a working royal without straying into party politics, which he constitutionally cannot do. It's a genuinely clever piece of positioning.

Homelessness — Where He Breaks From Tradition

William's homelessness work is the area where he most visibly differs from previous holders of the title.

The connection is personal — Princess Diana took him to homeless shelters as a child, and he has spoken publicly about how formative that was. His Homewards programme takes a notably ambitious position for a royal initiative: that homelessness can be ended, not merely managed.

That's a meaningfully different posture from traditional royal patronage, which typically means attending events and lending a name. Homewards commits to working with specific towns and cities on measurable outcomes over years.

It is also, quietly, a more politically exposed position than royals usually take. Declaring homelessness solvable implies it is a policy failure. He has stayed carefully on the right side of the constitutional line, but the ambition is notable.

The Constitutional Role — What He Cannot Do

The restrictions matter as much as the activities.

As heir, William cannot express party political opinions, cannot vote, and cannot comment on legislation before Parliament. He undertakes engagements on behalf of the monarch, represents the UK abroad, and supports charitable causes — all within strict conventions about neutrality.

He also holds military appointments and ceremonial roles, and stands in for the King at investitures and state occasions when required. That stand-in function has reportedly grown in recent years.

The tension in the modern role is obvious: he is expected to care about causes publicly while never advocating for the policies that would address them. Earthshot and Homewards are both designed to work within that constraint — focusing on solutions and delivery rather than on who should legislate what.

How His Approach Differs From King Charles

Charles spent decades as Prince of Wales writing to ministers, championing architecture, organic farming and traditional crafts — sometimes controversially.

William has been notably more disciplined. Fewer causes, pursued harder, with clearer metrics. Earthshot and Homewards are structured programmes with defined outcomes rather than broad areas of interest.

Reportedly, he has also signalled an intention to run a smaller, less ceremonial monarchy — fewer working royals, fewer formal occasions, more focus on a handful of initiatives. Whether that survives contact with the institution is one of the more interesting open questions about the next reign.

What to Watch Next

Three things worth following through the rest of 2026:

  • Duchy transparency. Any further disclosure about the estate's finances would be a genuine break with precedent.
  • Homewards results. The programme committed to measurable outcomes in specific locations. Those numbers will start arriving.
  • How much he deputises for the King. The frequency of stand-in engagements is the clearest available signal about the transition.
